questions.question: What are the four pillars of OOP and how do they work in Ruby?
questions.title: The Four Pillars of OOP
questions.direct_answer: The four pillars: Encapsulation (hide internal state, expose a clean interface — attr_accessor/attr_reader; private methods), Abstraction (model real things as classes with meaningful methods — a User with login, not a hash of data), Inheritance (a subclass reuses a parent's behavior — class Admin < User), Polymorphism (different objects respond to the same method their own way — duck typing, or overriding). Ruby does all four: encapsulation via private/protected and attr_*; abstraction via classes; inheritance via <; polymorphism via duck typing (no formal interfaces needed) and method overriding. They make code modular, reusable, and changeable.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can name the four pillars and map them to Ruby (encapsulation: private/attr_*; inheritance: <; polymorphism: duck typing/override).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking Ruby needs formal interfaces for polymorphism (it uses duck typing), or over-using inheritance where a module fits.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Four pillars: Encapsulation (private/attr_*), Abstraction (classes), Inheritance (<), Polymorphism (duck typing/override). Ruby does all four; polymorphism uses duck typing, not formal interfaces.

sections.title: Encapsulation, Abstraction, Inheritance, Polymorphism
sections.content: The four pillars: Encapsulation — hide internal state, expose a clean interface, with attr_accessor and attr_reader and private methods. Abstraction — model real things as classes with meaningful methods, a User with login rather than a hash of data. Inheritance — a subclass reuses a parent's behavior, class Admin less-than User. Polymorphism — different objects respond to the same method their own way, via duck typing or method overriding. Ruby does all four: encapsulation via private and protected and attr_star; abstraction via classes; inheritance via the angle bracket; and polymorphism via duck typing — no formal interfaces needed — and method overriding. They make code modular, reusable, and changeable.

sections.title: The Four Pillars
sections.content:
Each maps to a Ruby feature.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  E[Encapsulation: private/attr_*] --> A[Abstraction: classes]
  A --> I[Inheritance: <]
  I --> P[Polymorphism: duck typing/override]
```

sections.title: The four pillars in Ruby
sections.content:
```ruby
class Animal
  attr_reader :name                 # encapsulation: expose a reader
  def initialize(name); @name = name; end
  def speak; '...' end               # to be overridden (polymorphism)
  private
  def digest; end                    # encapsulation: hidden
end

class Dog < Animal                  # inheritance: reuse Animal
  def speak; 'Woof' end              # polymorphism: override speak
end

class Cat < Animal
  def speak; 'Meow' end
end

# Polymorphism via duck typing (no interface needed):
[Dog.new('Rex'), Cat.new('Tom')].each { |a| puts a.speak }  # Woof, Meow
# Any object with #speak works — that's duck typing.
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Thinking Ruby needs formal interfaces for polymorphism — it uses duck typing.
Over-using inheritance where a module would share the behavior better.
Exposing everything with attr_accessor when attr_reader is enough (over-exposure).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: The four pillars: Encapsulation, Abstraction, Inheritance, Polymorphism.
Encapsulation: hide state with private/protected and expose readers (attr_reader).
Abstraction: model real things as classes with meaningful methods.
Inheritance: a subclass reuses a parent's behavior with <.
Polymorphism: different objects respond to the same method (duck typing / override).
